summary:
Atlántico department sits under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report "Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia" records for the Atlántico department 54 intrafamily-violence cases, 41 sexual offences, 12 discrimination cases, 8 digital-violence cases, 69 threats, 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders and 8 lethal-violence cases. The report designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories with high threat levels for this population. It also reports that threats meet near-total impunity, with 99.8% of cases never advancing past the investigation stage.

The same report places Atlántico inside a national pattern: 270 LGBTIQ+ victims recorded in 2025, a 63% increase over the 165 recorded in 2024, equivalent to one killing every 32 hours. Violence is documented as a continuum running from discrimination through intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases) and threats (1,184 victims) to homicide and impunity, with territorial expansion of the violence into corridors of the illegal economy where state presence is weak, and an insufficient state response.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

On 4 April 2025 a 28-second video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was." President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise. The Atlántico departmental development plan and Barranquilla's development plan both commit to coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, the police and the judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.
tangentialFactors:
Atlántico is not an outlier within Colombia. Caribe Afirmativo's figures show the lethal violence documented in the department, including the two killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders, as part of a national count of 270 victims in 2025 that rose 63% over 2024, and the report describes the violence spreading into territories along illegal-economy corridors with weak state presence.

The department's proximity to organised armed activity echoes patterns recorded in Guajira and Caquetá, where flyer campaigns carrying kill lists and announced "social cleansing" campaigns have forced trans people, including a salon owner, to relocate repeatedly. Reporting on killings after the Millerey case frames them as calculated brutality continuing through the country's decades-long civil conflict rather than as isolated criminal acts.

Formal protections and their enforcement do not move together. The UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, praised Colombia's legal reforms in May 2025 while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience; Caribe Afirmativo's finding that 99.8% of threat cases never advance past the investigation stage points the same way.
localsOnly:
Changing the sex marker on a national identity card is an administrative act before a notary under the June 2015 rule change, not a court proceeding, and the route no longer requires bodily inspection or psychiatric assessment. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Atlántico's departmental development plan and Barranquilla's development plan obligate coordinated work with the Prosecutor's Office, police and judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people, giving residents a defined channel for complaints even where outcomes are rare.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree imposes procedural obligations on government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and for victims of armed conflict, and the May 2018 executive decree extends guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling permits transgender prisoners to choose their own hairstyle and makeup, and a subsequent ruling addresses the treatment of trans detainees.

For residents, recognition of foreign marriages is settled: the National Registry requires all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed abroad, with equal visa, healthcare, inheritance and pension treatment on presentation of a stamped certificate and identification papers. Marriage equality has existed since 2016 and joint adoption since 2015.
outOfScopeNotes:
Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report appears in two sources with different publication dates attached, one giving 27 September 2026 and the linked article carrying a May 2026 path; the report's own release date is not resolved here.

The figure of 270 victims in 2025 is reported alongside the 2024 comparison of 165 homicides and a rate of one killing every 32 hours, but the inventory does not make clear whether the 270 counts homicides or a wider class of victims. Both readings are carried as reported.

Whether the 99.8% impunity figure applies only to threat cases or to all the offence types catalogued in the Atlántico breakdown is not stated in the sources available here.

National sources record two killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders in Atlántico but do not name the victims, the dates or any investigation outcome; those cases remain unverified here.

Enforcement practice by Barranquilla and Soledad police in applying the premises-entry judgments and the Ministry of Interior decree, and any Atlántico-specific data on entry screening or document inspection at Rafael Núñez or Ernesto Cortissoz airports, are not sourced in this inventory.

Status of pending national legislation on gender identity and of any departmental anti-discrimination ordinance beyond the development-plan commitments is not sourced here.
